title: Epistemics: philosophy of science and calibration · Rung 1
subtitle: How strong is the evidence, how sure should you be, and how to say you were wrong
coverLine: Confidence that follows the evidence, written down, dated and changed out loud
subject: S59
author: Dr. Harsh Maheshwari

about.why: A clinician or researcher is asked every day how sure they are, and usually answers with a tone of voice. This book treats confidence as something that should follow the strength of the evidence, and teaches the difference between a hypothesis, a finding and a belief. It shows how to put a confidence on a claim in plain words and say why, and why being wrong in public is a normal event in science rather than a disgrace.
about.howToRead: Read Book 0 first, or at least the sections this book names as it goes. Then read this one in order. The book asks you to build one thing: a dated written record of five beliefs you hold about your own field, each with a confidence attached. Start it when the book tells you to and keep it; the next book in this subject scores it.
about.prerequisites: Book 0, in particular percentages (A4), ratios (A5), what a probability is (D1), the two-way table (D3), average and spread (D5), sampling (D6), random and systematic error (D7), reading a table (F1), checking a reference (F3) and the shape of an argument (F4). The mathematics is arithmetic with a calculator: turning a percentage into a fraction or odds and back, counting proportions in a small table, and filling a two-way table in natural frequencies. No algebra, no formula for Bayes’ theorem and no statistics beyond a mean, a range and, in the section on calibration, Book 0’s square-root law from sampling (D6), used to see how far chance moves a small tally of claims. You need something you have taught or written, and a notebook or file you will keep for the five dated beliefs.

blurb: A book on how much to believe. It covers why evidence comes in strengths, how a hypothesis differs from a finding and both from a belief, how to state a confidence in words that mean the same thing to every reader, how to change a position when the evidence changes, and why saying "I was wrong about that" is part of the work.

One finding, several explanations
Belief beyond the evidence

Why evidence comes in strengths
GRADE certainty: four levels, where you start, and moving down or up
Certainty of the evidence is not the strength of a recommendation, and certainty has words
No evidence of an effect is not evidence of no effect
Confidence as a probability: putting a number on how sure you are of one claim
The same word read as different numbers
Calibrated scales: fixing what the words mean, and putting the number beside the word
Stating how confident you are, and saying why
The base rate: how often claims like this one hold up
Updating: changing your confidence by as much as the evidence warrants
Confidence is not accuracy: what being calibrated means
Changing a stated position out loud
How science corrects its record: correction, expression of concern, retraction, republication
Being wrong in public is common, and owning it costs less than hiding it
Saying “I was wrong about that”
The dated belief register: what you believe, how sure you are, and when you said it
Worked journey: One claim, from a belief to a dated line: “eating breakfast helps you lose weight”
